On 29 June 2014 the jihadist group known as ISIS, the Islamic State of Iraq and Syria, declared a caliphate over the lands it held in Iraq and Syria. Days later its leader, Abu Bakr al-Baghdadi, appeared in the great mosque of Mosul to claim the title of caliph.

The group grew out of al-Qaeda in Iraq, born in the chaos after the 2003 US-led invasion that removed Saddam Hussein. It rebuilt itself in the Syrian civil war, then swept across northern Iraq in June 2014, taking Mosul as the Iraqi army fled.

At its height it ruled about a third of Iraq and Syria and millions of people, with its capital at Raqqa. It enslaved and massacred Yazidis, killed Shia and Christians, filmed beheadings and drew tens of thousands of foreign fighters.

It claimed to restore the office ended by the abolition of the caliphate in 1924; almost all Muslim scholars rejected it. A US-led coalition, Iraqi forces and Kurdish fighters took back its land, ending with the fall of Baghuz in Syria in 2019.
